Problem 7.92 Lesson 18 · p. 487 · §7.4

Designing the classical single-supply MOSFET bias circuit (gate voltage divider plus source resistor).

Problem statement

D 7.92 Consider the classical biasing scheme shown in Fig. 7.50(c), using a 9-V supply. For the MOSFET, Vt=0.7 V, λ=0, and kn=5mA/V2. Arrange that the drain current is 0.2 mA, with about one-third of the supply voltage across each of RS and RD. Use 22 MΩ for the larger of RG1 and RG2. What are the values of RG1, RG2, RS, and RD that you have chosen? Specify them to two significant digits. For your design, how far is the drain voltage from the edge of saturation?

The problem has no figure of its own; it uses Fig. 7.50(c), shown below. It is marked with the video-example icon VE 7.2 (same problem with different numbers, p. 454).

Similar to 7.92 same circuit, new numbers · classical single-supply bias · Fig. 7.50(c)

Design the divider-plus-source-resistor bias, then check the margin to the edge of saturation.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Consider the classical biasing scheme of Fig. 7.50(c), using a 12-V supply. For the MOSFET, Vt=1.0 V, λ=0, and kn=2mA/V2. Arrange that the drain current is 0.5 mA, with about one-third of the supply voltage across each of RS and RD. Use 20 MΩ for the larger of RG1 and RG2. Find RG1, RG2, RS, and RD to two significant digits. How far is the drain voltage from the edge of saturation?

Step 1 · Overdrive and VGS from the required current

From Eq. (7.25), ID=12knVOV2, so

VOV=2IDkn=2(0.5)2=0.707V,VGS=Vt+VOV=1.707V
Step 2 · Apply the one-third rule

One-third of 12 V is 4 V across each of RD, the transistor, and RS. So VS=4 V and VD=12−4=8 V.

RS=VSID=40.5=8.0kΩ,RD=VDD−VDID=12−80.5=8.0kΩ
Step 3 · Required gate voltage

Eq. (7.137): VG=VGS+RSID=VGS+VS.

VG=1.707+4=5.707V
Step 4 · Size the divider

Because IG=0, the divider is unloaded: VG=VDDRG2/(RG1+RG2). Here VG is a bit less than half of 12 V, so the top resistor RG1 must be the larger one. Set RG1=20 MΩ:

RG2=RG1VGVDD−VG=20×5.7076.293=18.1MΩ→18MΩ
Step 5 · Recompute the bias with the rounded values

With RG1=20 MΩ and RG2=18 MΩ, VG=12×18/38=5.684 V. Combine VG=Vt+VOV+RS·12knVOV2:

5.684=1+VOV+8VOV2⇒8VOV2+VOV−4.684=0⇒VOV=0.705V

(Take the positive root.) Then ID=12(2)(0.705)2=0.497 mA, VS=8(0.497)=3.98 V and VD=12−8(0.497)=8.02 V. That is close to the targets, so the rounding is fine.

Step 6 · Distance from the edge of saturation

The triode boundary is where vDS=vGS−Vt. With the gate fixed at VG, the drain can fall to VG−Vt (p. 452):

VG−Vt=5.684−1=4.684VVD−(VG−Vt)=8.02−4.68=3.34V

Check: VDS−VOV=(8.02−3.98)−0.705=3.34 V, which matches.

Answers (similar problem)
RG1, RG220 MΩ, 18 MΩ
RS, RD8.0 kΩ, 8.0 kΩ
Actual biasID≈0.50 mA, VD≈8.0 V
Drain above the edge of saturation≈ 3.3 V

Expansion note: why there is no W/L to find here

The book writes the MOSFET's strength in two ways: the process parameter kn′ times the aspect ratio W/L, or the single device parameter kn=kn′(W/L). When a problem gives kn itself, the aspect ratio is already folded in, so W/L never appears.

Why bias design matters §7.4, pp. 448–449

Summarized

Bias design sets a dc drain current that is predictable and insensitive to temperature and to the large spread in parameters between devices of the same type (for discrete MOSFETs, especially Vt). A second goal is to put the operating point in the active (saturation) region so the amplifier has high gain while allowing the required output signal swing without leaving saturation. The section neglects the Early effect (λ=0, VA=∞).

Biasing by fixing VG and connecting a resistance in the source §7.4.1, pp. 449–451

Quoted · p. 449

An excellent biasing technique for discrete MOSFET circuits consists of fixing the dc voltage at the gate, VG, and connecting a resistance in the source lead, as shown in Fig. 7.50(a). For this circuit,

VG=VGS+RSID
(7.137)
Quoted · p. 451

Now, if VG is much greater than VGS, ID will be mostly determined by the values of VG and RS. However, even if VG is not much larger than VGS, resistor RS provides negative feedback, which acts to stabilize the value of the bias current ID. …

Two possible practical discrete implementations of this bias scheme are shown in Figs. 7.50(c) and (e). The circuit in Fig. 7.50(c) uses one power-supply VDD and derives VG through a voltage divider (RG1,RG2). Since IG=0, RG1 and RG2 can be selected to be very large (in the megohm range), allowing the MOSFET to present a large input resistance to a signal source that may be connected to the gate through a coupling capacitor, as shown in Fig. 7.50(d). … Finally, note that in the circuit of Fig. 7.50(c), resistor RD is selected to be as large as possible to obtain high gain but small enough to allow for the desired signal swing at the drain while keeping the MOSFET in saturation at all times.

Expansion note: why a source resistor steadies the bias current

With the gate voltage fixed, any rise in ID raises the drop RSID, which lifts the source and leaves less VGS. Less VGS pushes ID back down. This self-correction is the negative feedback the book mentions, and it is why two devices with different Vt end up with similar currents (Fig. 7.50b).

Worked example: designing Fig. 7.50(c) Example 7.11, pp. 451–453

Quoted · Example 7.11 statement

We need to design the circuit of Fig. 7.50(c) to establish a dc drain current ID=0.5 mA. The MOSFET is specified to have Vt=1 V and kn′W/L=1mA/V2. For simplicity, neglect the Early effect (i.e., assume λ=0). Use a power-supply VDD=15 V. Calculate the percentage change in the value of ID when the MOSFET is replaced with another unit having the same kn′W/L but Vt=1.5 V.

Quoted · Example 7.11 solution, p. 452

As a rule of thumb for designing this classical biasing circuit, we choose RD and RS to provide one-third of the power-supply voltage VDD as a drop across each of RD, the transistor (i.e., VDS), and RS. For VDD=15 V, this choice makes VD=+10 V and VS=+5 V. Now, since ID is required to be 0.5 mA, we can find the values of RD and RS as follows:

RD=VDD−VDID=15−100.5=10kΩRS=VSID=50.5=10kΩ

The required value of VGS can be determined by first calculating the overdrive voltage VOV from

ID=12kn′(W/L)VOV20.5=12×1×VOV2

which gives VOV=1 V, and thus, VGS=Vt+VOV=1+1=2 V. Now, since VS=+5 V, VG must be VG=VS+VGS=5+2=7 V.

To establish this voltage at the gate, we can select RG1=8 MΩ and RG2=7 MΩ. The final circuit is shown in Fig. 7.51. Observe that the dc voltage at the drain (+10 V) allows for a positive signal swing of +5 V (i.e., up to VDD) and a negative signal swing of 4 V [i.e., down to (VG−Vt)].

Expansion note: what the one-third rule of thumb is for

Splitting VDD roughly equally across RD, the transistor and RS is a starting point, not a law. The drop across RS buys bias stability, the drop across RD buys gain and room for the drain to swing up, and the VDS third keeps the transistor clear of the triode region while the drain swings down.

Summarized (rest of Example 7.11, pp. 452–453)

For the second device (Vt=1.5 V) the book writes ID=12×1×(VGS−1.5)2 (7.138) and 7=VGS+10ID (7.139), solves them together to get ID=0.455 mA, a −9% change.

Arrange that the drain current is 1 mA, with about one-third of the supply voltage across each of RS and RD. Use 22 MΩ for the larger of RG1 and RG2. What are the values of RG1, RG2, RS, and RD that you have chosen? Specify them to two significant digits. For your design, how far is the drain voltage from the edge of saturation?

“Related end-of-chapter problem: 7.92.” No printed answers.

Choosing where the bias point sits §7.1.7, p. 380

Summarized

Placing Q near the triode boundary raises gain but limits the negative swing at the drain; placing it near VDD limits the positive swing. Point Q1 in Fig. 7.9 lacks “headroom” (positive peaks clip as the MOSFET turns off); point Q2 lacks “legroom” (negative peaks push the MOSFET into triode).

Expansion note: what headroom and legroom mean

Headroom is the space above the bias point before the drain reaches VDD and the transistor cuts off; legroom is the space below it before the transistor enters triode. A bias point placed for large gain often trades away one of the two.

The saturation condition §7.2.1, p. 381

Quoted
ID=12kn(VGS−Vt)2=12knVOV2
(7.25)

where we have neglected channel-length modulation (i.e., we have assumed λ=0). Here VOV=VGS−Vt is the overdrive voltage at which the MOSFET is biased to operate. … To ensure saturation-region operation, we must have VDS>VOV.

Expansion note: what "the edge of saturation" means

The saturation region ends where vDS=vGS−Vt, that is, where VDS has shrunk to the overdrive voltage. Below that line the device is in triode.

Problem 7.103 Lesson 18 · p. 489 · §7.4

A drain-to-gate feedback bias circuit whose feedback resistor is split into a divider.

Problem statement

D 7.103 Figure P7.103 shows a variation of the feedback-bias circuit of Fig. 7.52. Using a 3-V supply with an NMOS transistor for which Vt=0.8 V, kn=4mA/V2, and λ=0, provide a design that biases the transistor at ID=0.5 mA, with VDS large enough to allow saturation operation for a 1-V negative signal swing at the drain. Use 13 MΩ as the largest resistor in the feedback-bias network. What values of RD, RG1, and RG2 have you chosen?

Similar to 7.103 same circuit, new numbers · feedback bias with a divider · Fig. P7.103

Pick RD, RG1, RG2 so the drain has room for a given negative swing.

Similar problem (new numbers)

For the circuit of Fig. P7.103, use a 5-V supply and an NMOS transistor with Vt=1.0 V, kn=2mA/V2, and λ=0. Bias the transistor at ID=0.4 mA, with VDS large enough to allow saturation operation for a 1.5-V negative signal swing at the drain. Use 15 MΩ as the largest resistor in the feedback-bias network. Find RD, RG1, and RG2.

Step 1 · Overdrive and VGS
VOV=2(0.4)2=0.632V,VGS=1+0.632=1.632V

The source is grounded, so VG=VGS=1.632 V.

Step 2 · Lowest allowed drain voltage → required dc VD

To stay in saturation, vDS≥vGS−Vt. Treating the gate at its dc value (the convention of Example 7.11), the drain may fall only to VG−Vt=VOV=0.632 V. The drain must be able to swing 1.5 V below its dc level and still be at or above that:

VD−1.5≥0.632⇒VD=2.132V

Use the minimum. A lower VD means a larger RD, and the largest RD gives the most gain.

Step 3 · Drain resistor

KCL at the drain: RD carries ID plus the divider current VD/(RG1+RG2). The divider current is about 0.1 μA, negligible against 0.4 mA:

RD=VDD−VDID=5−2.1320.4=7.17kΩ→7.2kΩ
Step 4 · Feedback divider

With IG=0: VG=VDRG2/(RG1+RG2). The ratio VG/VD=1.632/2.132=0.766 is more than one-half, so RG2 is the larger resistor. Set RG2=15 MΩ:

RG1=RG2VD−VGVG=15×0.5001.632=4.6MΩ
Step 5 · Check with the chosen values

With RD=7.2 kΩ, RG1=4.6 MΩ, RG2=15 MΩ, solve VD=5−7.2ID together with ID=12(2)(0.765VD−1)2. This gives VD=2.13 V, VG=1.63 V, ID=0.398 mA. The room below VD is VD−(VG−Vt)=1.50 V, as required.

Note · Note on the gate signal

Steps 2–5 treat the gate as staying at its dc voltage while the drain swings, as Example 7.11 does. If the input signal also drives the gate (as in Example 7.3), the gate rises while the drain falls. That uses up some extra room, roughly 1.5/(gmRD)≈1.5/9.1≈0.17 V here. To include it, add that amount to VD in Step 2.

Answers (similar problem)
RD7.2 kΩ
RG1 (drain to gate)4.6 MΩ
RG2 (gate to ground)15 MΩ
Resulting biasVD≈2.13 V, VG≈1.63 V, ID≈0.40 mA

Biasing using a drain-to-gate feedback resistor §7.4.1, pp. 454–455

Quoted · p. 454

Figure 7.52 shows a simple and effective discrete-circuit biasing arrangement using a feedback resistor connected between the drain and the gate. Here the large feedback resistance RG (usually in the megohm range) forces the dc voltage at the gate to be equal to that at the drain (because IG=0). Thus we can write

VGS=VDS=VDD−RDID

which can be rewritten

VDD=VGS+RDID
(7.140)

This is identical in form to Eq. (7.137), which describes the operation of the bias scheme discussed above [that in Fig. 7.50(a)]. Thus, here too, if ID for some reason changes, say increases, then Eq. (7.140) indicates that VGS must decrease. The decrease in VGS in turn causes a decrease in ID, a change that is opposite in direction to the one we originally assumed. Thus the negative feedback or degeneration provided by RG works to keep the value of ID as constant as possible.

The circuit of Fig. 7.52 can be used as an amplifier by applying the input voltage signal to the gate via a coupling capacitor so as not to disturb the dc bias conditions already established. The amplified output signal at the drain can be coupled to another part of the circuit, again via a capacitor. We considered such an amplifier circuit in Section 7.2 (Example 7.3).

Expansion note: why no dc voltage drops across the feedback resistor

The gate of a MOSFET draws no dc current (IG=0). A resistor that carries no current has no voltage across it, so the gate end and the drain end of RG sit at the same dc voltage. That is why the book can write VGS=VDS for Fig. 7.52.

Worked example: the feedback-biased amplifier Example 7.3, pp. 388–392

The book ends this example with: “A modification of this circuit that increases the allowable signal swing is investigated in Problem 7.103.”

Quoted · Example 7.3 statement, pp. 388–389

Figure 7.16(a) shows a discrete MOSFET amplifier biased with a drain-to-gate resistance RG. We will study this biasing arrangement in Section 7.4. The input signal vi is coupled to the gate via a large capacitor, and the output signal at the drain is coupled to the load resistance RL via another large capacitor. We want to analyze this amplifier circuit to determine its small-signal voltage gain, its input resistance, and the largest allowable input signal. The transistor has Vt=1.5 V, kn′(W/L)=0.25mA/V2, and VA=50 V. Assume that the coupling capacitors are large enough that they act as short circuits at the signal frequencies of interest.

Expansion note: how the three circuit pictures in Fig. 7.16 relate

Part (a) is the real amplifier. Part (b) keeps only what matters for dc: capacitors become open circuits and the signal source is removed. Parts (c) and (d) keep only what matters for the signal: capacitors become short circuits, VDD becomes ground, and the MOSFET becomes its small-signal model.

Quoted · dc operating point, p. 390

We first determine the dc operating point. For this purpose, we eliminate the input signal vi, and open-circuit the two coupling capacitors (since they block dc currents). The result is the circuit shown in Fig. 7.16(b). We note that since IG=0, the dc voltage drop across RG will be zero, and

VGS=VDS=VDD−RDID
(7.43)

With VDS=VGS, the NMOS transistor will operate in saturation. Thus,

ID=12kn(VGS−Vt)2
(7.44)

… Substituting VDD=15 V, RD=10 kΩ, kn=0.25mA/V2, and Vt=1.5 V in Eqs. (7.43) and (7.44), and substituting for VGS from Eq. (7.43) into Eq. (7.44) results in a quadratic equation in ID. Solving it and discarding the root that is not physically meaningful yields the solution ID=1.06 mA, which corresponds to VGS=VDS=4.4 V and VOV=4.4−1.5=2.9 V.

Summarized (small-signal part, pp. 390–391)

With gm=knVOV=0.725 mA/V and ro=VA/ID=47 kΩ, the book combines R′L=RL∥RD∥ro=4.52 kΩ and finds Av≃−gmR′L=−3.3 V/V (Eq. 7.47) and Rin=RG/(1+gmR′L)=2.33 MΩ (Eq. 7.48).

Quoted · largest allowable signal, pp. 391–392

The largest allowable input signal v^i is constrained by the need to keep the transistor in saturation at all times; that is,

vDS≥vGS−Vt

We can enforce this condition by making the two terms equal at the point vGS is maximum and vDS is minimum,

vDSmin=vGSmax−VtVDS−|Av|v^i=VGS+v^i−Vt

Since VDS=VGS, we obtain

v^i=Vt|Av|+1

This is a general relationship that applies to this circuit irrespective of the component values. Observe that it simply states that the maximum signal swing is determined by the fact that the bias arrangement makes VD=VG and thus, to keep the MOSFET out of the triode region, the maximum signal between D and G is constrained to be equal to Vt. For our particular design, v^i=1.5/(3.3+1)=0.35 V.

Expansion note: why the worst moment is gate-high, drain-low

This amplifier inverts: when the gate signal rises, the drain signal falls, by |Av| times as much. Saturation needs the drain to stay above the gate by no less than −Vt. The gap between them is smallest when the gate is at its positive peak and the drain at its negative peak, so that instant sets the limit.

Saturation limits on the instantaneous voltages §7.2.1, p. 384

Expansion note: how to read Fig. 7.12

The upper waveform is the total gate-to-source voltage, a dc level with a small signal on top. The lower one is the total drain-to-source voltage, larger and upside down. The two annotations mark the limits: the top of vDS must stay below VDD, and its bottom must stay above the matching vGS peak minus Vt.

Quoted · p. 384

For operation in the saturation (active) region at all times, the minimum value of vDS should not fall below the corresponding value of vGS by more than Vt. Also, the maximum value of vDS should be smaller than VDD; otherwise the FET will enter the cutoff region and the peaks of the output signal waveform will be clipped off.

Find VOV, ID, RD, and RG to obtain a voltage gain of −25 V/V and an input resistance of 0.5 MΩ. What is the maximum allowable input signal, v^i?

Problem 7.118 Lesson 19 · p. 491 · §7.5

A capacitively coupled common-source amplifier: bias check, gain, maximum signal, and adding source degeneration.

Problem statement

SIM 7.118 The NMOS transistor in the CS amplifier shown in Fig. 7.57(a) has Vt=0.75 V and VA=50 V. Also, VDD=5 V, RG1=750 kΩ, RG2=500 kΩ, RD=10 kΩ, RS=4 kΩ, Rsig=100 kΩ, and RL=10 kΩ.

  1. Neglecting the Early effect, verify that the MOSFET is operating in saturation with ID=0.25 mA and VOV=0.25 V. What must the MOSFET's kn be? What is the dc voltage at the drain?
  2. Find Rin and Gv.
  3. If vsig is a sinusoid with a peak amplitude v^sig, find the maximum allowable value of v^sig for which the transistor remains in saturation. What is the corresponding amplitude of the output voltage?
  4. What is the value of resistance R that needs to be inserted in series with capacitor CS in order to allow us to double the input signal v^sig? What output voltage now results?

The problem has no figure of its own; it uses Fig. 7.57(a), shown below with the book's bias circuit (b) and equivalent circuit (c).

Similar to 7.118 same circuit, new numbers · CS amplifier · Fig. 7.57(a)

Bias check, Rin and Gv, the largest input signal, and adding an unbypassed source resistor.

Similar problem (new numbers)

The NMOS transistor in the CS amplifier of Fig. 7.57(a) has Vt=0.6 V and VA=40 V. Also, VDD=6 V, RG1=1.2 MΩ, RG2=0.8 MΩ, RD=12 kΩ, RS=5 kΩ, Rsig=200 kΩ, and RL=12 kΩ.

  1. Neglecting the Early effect, verify that the MOSFET is in saturation with ID=0.3 mA and VOV=0.3 V. What is kn? What is the dc drain voltage?
  2. Find Rin and Gv.
  3. Find the largest v^sig for which the transistor stays in saturation, and the corresponding output amplitude.
  4. What resistance R in series with CS lets v^sig be doubled? What output amplitude results?

(a) Bias

Step 1 · Gate and source voltages
VG=6×0.81.2+0.8=2.4V,VS=IDRS=0.3×5=1.5V

So VGS=2.4−1.5=0.9 V and VOV=0.9−0.6=0.3 V, which is consistent with Eq. (7.137).

Step 2 · kn from Eq. (7.25)
kn=2IDVOV2=2(0.3)0.32=6.67mA/V2
Step 3 · Drain voltage and saturation check
VD=6−0.3×12=2.4V,VDS=2.4−1.5=0.9V>VOV=0.3V✓

(b) Rin and Gv

Step 4 · Small-signal parameters
gm=2IDVOV=0.60.3=2mA/V,ro=VAID=400.3=133kΩ
Step 5 · Input resistance and overall gain
Rin=1.2∥0.8=0.48MΩ,RD∥RL∥ro=12∥12∥133=5.74kΩ
Gv=−480480+200(2)(5.74)=−0.706×11.48=−8.1V/V
Eq. (7.150)

The gate-to-output gain alone is Av=−gm(RD∥RL∥ro)=−11.48 V/V. It is used in the next step.

(c) Largest input signal

Step 6 · Write the saturation condition at the worst instant

The source is at signal ground (because of CS), so vDS−vGS=vD−vG. Saturation needs vD−vG≥−Vt. The worst instant is when the gate is at its positive peak and the drain at its negative peak:

(VD−|Av|v^gs)−(VG+v^gs)=−Vt⇒v^gs=VD−VG+Vt|Av|+1=2.4−2.4+0.612.48=48.1mV

This is Example 7.3's method (p. 392). Here the gate and drain dc voltages happen to be equal, so the available room is exactly Vt.

Step 7 · Refer back to the source, then find the output
v^sig=v^gsRin+RsigRin=48.1×680480=68mV,v^o=|Av|v^gs=11.48×0.0481=0.55V

Checks: v^o=|Gv|v^sig=8.1×0.068=0.55 V. Also, 48 mV is well under 2VOV=0.6 V, and the top of the swing (2.4 + 0.55 V) stays below VDD.

(d) Unbypassed source resistor

Step 8 · What R changes

R in series with CS carries the signal current, so it acts as a source-degeneration resistance Rs=R (§7.3.4). Now only vgs=vi/(1+gmR) appears across gate–source (Eq. 7.98), and the drain swing is |Av|vi/(1+gmR). For the source-degenerated case, ro is kept lumped into the 5.74 kΩ load as an approximation; p. 448 says its effect there is small.

Step 9 · Same saturation room, double the input

vDS−vGS=vD−vG still holds, because vS cancels. The condition becomes

VD−VG+Vt=v^i(|Av|1+gmR+1)

With v^i doubled to 2×48.1=96.1 mV:

0.6=0.0961(11.481+gmR+1)⇒1+gmR=2.19⇒R=1.192=0.60kΩ
Step 10 · New output
v^o=gm(RD∥RL∥ro)1+gmRv^i=11.482.19×0.0961=0.50V
Eq. (7.103)

The new overall gain is Gv=−0.706×11.48/2.19=−3.7 V/V. With v^sig=136 mV, v^o=3.7×0.136=0.50 V. The output is a little smaller than before, the same lesson as the Comment after Exercise 7.22.

Note · A simpler reading of (d)

Some solutions keep v^gs unchanged when the input doubles, as Exercise 7.23 does. That needs 1+gmR=2, so R=1/gm=0.5 kΩ, and the output stays at 0.55 V. That criterion keeps distortion the same. The answer above instead keeps the transistor exactly at the edge of saturation. Use whichever your instructor intends.

Answers (similar problem)
(a)Saturated (VDS=0.9 V > 0.3 V); kn=6.67mA/V2; VD=2.4 V
(b)Rin=480 kΩ; Gv=−8.1 V/V
(c)v^sig,max≈68 mV; v^o≈0.55 V
(d)R≈0.60 kΩ (saturation-edge criterion); v^o≈0.50 V

The common-source amplifier §7.5.1, pp. 461–463

Quoted · pp. 461–462

As mentioned in Section 7.3, the common-source (CS) configuration is the most widely used of all MOSFET amplifier circuits. A common-source amplifier using the bias circuit of Fig. 7.50(c) is shown in Fig. 7.57(a). Notice that to establish a signal ground (sometimes called an ac ground) at the source, we have connected a large capacitor, CS, between the source and ground. This capacitor, usually in the microfarad range, is required to provide a very small impedance (ideally, zero impedance—in effect, a short circuit) at all signal frequencies of interest. In this way, the signal current passes through CS to ground and thus bypasses the resistance RS; hence, CS is called a bypass capacitor. … For our purposes here we will assume that CS is acting as a perfect short circuit and thus is establishing a zero signal voltage at the MOSFET source.

Expansion note: what "signal ground" means

A signal ground is a node whose voltage does not change with the signal, even though it may sit at a nonzero dc voltage. The bypass capacitor holds the source steady for signals, so in the small-signal circuit the source is drawn connected to ground.

Quoted · p. 463

Since a capacitor behaves as an open circuit at dc, the circuit for performing the dc bias design and analysis is obtained by open-circuiting all capacitors. The resulting circuit is shown in Fig. 7.57(b) and can be designed as discussed in Section 7.4.1.

To determine the characteristics of the CS amplifier of Fig. 7.57(a)—that is, its input resistance, voltage gain, and output resistance—we replace the MOSFET with its hybrid-π small-signal model, replace VDD with a signal ground, and replace all coupling and bypass capacitors with short circuits. The result is the circuit in Fig. 7.57(c). Analysis is straightforward and is shown on the figure, thus

Rin=RG1∥RG2
(7.149)

which shows that to keep Rin high, large values should be used for RG1 and RG2, usually in the megohm range. The overall voltage gain Gv is

Gv=−RinRin+Rsiggm(RD∥RL∥ro)
(7.150)

Notice that we have taken ro into account, simply because it is easy to do so. Its effect, however, is usually small …

Expansion note: why the dc and signal circuits are analyzed separately

Because the small-signal model is linear, the dc bias and the signal can be found one at a time and added. For dc, capacitors are open and only the supply acts. For the signal, capacitors and the supply act as shorts to ground and only the signal source acts.

Neglecting the Early effect, design for ID=0.5 mA, VS=3.5 V, and VD=6 V using a power-supply VDD=15 V. Specify the values of RS and RD. If a current of 2 μA is used in the voltage divider, specify the values of RG1 and RG2. Give the values of the MOSFET parameters gm and ro at the bias point.

Small-signal parameters gm and ro §7.2.1, pp. 383–387

Quoted · p. 383

The parameter that relates id and vgs is the MOSFET transconductance gm,

gm≡idvgs=kn(VGS−Vt)
(7.32)

or in terms of the overdrive voltage VOV,

gm=knVOV
(7.33)
Quoted · p. 385

… the drain current does in fact depend on vDS in a linear manner. Such dependence was modeled by a finite resistance ro between drain and source, whose value was given by Eq. (5.27) in Section 5.2.4, which we repeat here (with the prime on ID dropped) as

ro=|VA|ID
(7.37)

where the Early voltage VA=1/λ is a MOSFET parameter that either is specified or can be measured.

Quoted · p. 387

Yet another useful expression for gm of the MOSFET can be obtained by substituting for kn′(W/L) in Eq. (7.40) by 2ID/(VGS−Vt)2:

gm=2IDVGS−Vt=2IDVOV=ID(VOV/2)
(7.42)
Expansion note: why the book gives several formulas for gm

Equations (7.32), (7.33) and (7.42) are the same transconductance at the same bias point, written with different known quantities: one uses kn and the overdrive, another uses ID and the overdrive. They give the same number when the bias values are consistent.

Maximum signal before leaving saturation §7.2.1, pp. 382–384

Quoted · p. 382

To reduce the nonlinear distortion introduced by the MOSFET, the input signal should be kept small so that … vgs≪2(VGS−Vt) (7.29) or, equivalently,

vgs≪2VOV
(7.30)
Quoted · p. 384

For operation in the saturation (active) region at all times, the minimum value of vDS should not fall below the corresponding value of vGS by more than Vt. Also, the maximum value of vDS should be smaller than VDD; otherwise the FET will enter the cutoff region and the peaks of the output signal waveform will be clipped off.

Summarized · Example 7.3, pp. 391–392

Example 7.3 (quoted in full under Problem 7.103) shows how the book turns this into a number: it writes vDSmin=vGSmax−Vt, substitutes the dc values plus the signal peaks (VDS−|Av|v^i=VGS+v^i−Vt), and solves for v^i. Note that in that circuit the source is grounded and the gate-to-drain gain is Av; in Fig. 7.57 the source is held at signal ground by CS.

Quoted · Example 7.8, p. 426 (BJT, but same input-to-output scaling)

If the maximum amplitude of vπ is to be 5 mV, the corresponding value of v^sig is

v^sig=(Rin+RsigRin)v^π

and the amplitude of the signal at the output is v^o=Gvv^sig.

Expansion note: what a hat over a symbol means

A hat marks a peak amplitude: v^sig is the peak value of the sinusoid vsig. Peak values scale through a linear amplifier by the same gain as the instantaneous signals.

Including ro §7.3.8, p. 448

Quoted

In the CS and CE amplifiers, we can see that ro of the transistor appears in parallel with RD and RC, respectively, and can be simply included in the corresponding formulas by replacing RD with (RD∥ro) and RC with (RC∥ro). The effect will be a reduction in the magnitude of gain, of perhaps 5% to 10%. … There are configurations in which taking ro into account complicates the analysis considerably. These are the CS (CE) amplifier with a source (emitter) resistance, and the CG (CB) amplifier. Fortunately, for discrete implementation of these configurations, the effect of neglecting ro is usually small …

CS amplifier with a source resistance (for part d) §7.3.4, pp. 427–429

Quoted · p. 427

It is often beneficial to insert a resistance Rs … in the source lead … of a common-source … amplifier. Figure 7.38(a) shows a CS amplifier with a resistance Rs in its source lead. The corresponding small-signal equivalent circuit is shown in Fig. 7.38(b), where we have used the T model for the MOSFET. … In general, whenever a resistance is connected in the source lead, the T model is preferred. The source resistance then appears in series with the model resistance 1/gm and can be added to it.

Quoted · pp. 428–429

… only a fraction of vi appears between gate and source as vgs. The voltage divider composed of 1/gm and Rs can be used to determine vgs, as follows:

vgs=vi1/gm1/gm+Rs=vi1+gmRs
(7.98)

Thus we can use the value of Rs to control the magnitude of the signal vgs and thereby ensure that vgs does not become too large and cause unacceptably high nonlinear distortion. …

i=vi1/gm+Rs=(gm1+gmRs)vi
(7.99)
Avo≡vovi=−gmRD1+gmRs
(7.100)
Avo=−RD1/gm+Rs
(7.101)

Equation (7.100) indicates that including the resistance Rs reduces the voltage gain by the factor (1+gmRs). … Because of the negative-feedback action of Rs it is known as a source-degeneration resistance.

Voltage gain from gate to drain=−Total resistance in drainTotal resistance in source
(7.102)

… we can find Av by simply replacing RD in Eq. (7.101) or (7.100) by (RD∥RL); thus,

Av=−gm(RD∥RL)1+gmRs
(7.103)
Av=−RD∥RL1/gm+Rs
(7.104)
Expansion note: what source degeneration trades

A resistance in the source lead that carries signal current reduces the gain by the factor (1+gmRs) and lets only a fraction of the input appear across gate and source. In return the circuit accepts a larger input before distortion or saturation limits are reached, and the gain depends less on the device.

Problem 7.121 Lesson 19 · p. 492 · §7.5

Two-supply bias design (gate resistor to ground, source resistor to −VSS) with a required drain swing.

Problem statement

D *7.121 The MOSFET in the circuit of Fig. P7.121 has Vt=0.8 V, kn=5mA/V2, and VA=40 V.

  1. Find the values of RS, RD, and RG so that ID=0.4 mA, the largest possible value for RD is used while a maximum signal swing at the drain of ±0.8 V is possible, and the input resistance at the gate is 10 MΩ. Neglect the Early effect.
  2. Find the values of gm and ro at the bias point.
  3. If terminal Z is grounded, terminal X is connected to a signal source with a resistance of 1 MΩ, and terminal Y is connected to a load resistance of 10 kΩ, find the voltage gain from signal source to load.
  4. If terminal Y is grounded, find the voltage gain from X to Z with Z open-circuited. What is the output resistance of the source follower?
  5. If terminal X is grounded and terminal Z is connected to a current source delivering a signal current of 50 μA and having a resistance of 100 kΩ, find the voltage signal that can be measured at Y. For simplicity, neglect the effect of ro.

Assigned parts: (a). The reading, toolkit and worked similar problem below cover part (a) only.

Expansion note: what the ∞ capacitors and terminals X, Y, Z are for

A capacitor marked ∞ is large enough to be an open circuit at dc and a short circuit at signal frequencies. The terminals X, Y and Z let the same biased transistor be used in different configurations by connecting a source, a load or ground to them; for the dc design every capacitor is simply open.

Similar to 7.121(a) same circuit, new numbers · two-supply bias · Fig. P7.121 / 7.50(e)

Choose RS, the largest RD for a given drain swing, and RG for a given input resistance.

Similar problem (new numbers)

The MOSFET in a circuit like Fig. P7.121, but with supplies of +6 V and −6 V, has Vt=1.0 V, kn=4mA/V2, and VA=50 V. Find RS, RD, and RG so that ID=0.5 mA, the largest possible RD is used while a maximum drain swing of ±1.0 V is possible, and the input resistance at the gate is 5 MΩ. Neglect the Early effect.

Step 1 · Overdrive and VGS
VOV=2(0.5)4=0.5V,VGS=1.0+0.5=1.5V
Step 2 · Source resistor

No gate current flows through RG, so VG=0 and VS=−VGS=−1.5 V. By Ohm's law across RS down to −6 V:

RS=VS−(−VSS)ID=−1.5+60.5=9.0kΩ

Equivalently, Eq. (7.137) with VG replaced by VSS: 6=1.5+0.5RS.

Step 3 · Lowest drain voltage the swing can reach

The triode edge for the drain is VG−Vt=0−1=−1 V (gate taken at its dc value, as in Example 7.11). A −1.0 V swing must not go below that:

VD−1.0≥−1.0⇒VD≥0V

The largest RD gives the lowest VD, so choose VD=0 V. The +1.0 V peak (to +1 V) stays well under the +6 V supply, so the cutoff side is not the limit.

Step 4 · Drain resistor
RD=VDD−VDID=6−00.5=12kΩ
Step 5 · Gate resistor

The gate draws no current, and the capacitor from X is a short for signals. The resistance seen at the gate is therefore just RG to ground (p. 451), so RG=5 MΩ.

Answers (similar problem)
RS9.0 kΩ (VS=−1.5 V)
RD12 kΩ (VD=0 V)
RG5 MΩ

The two-supply version of the fixed-VG scheme §7.4.1, p. 451

Quoted

When two power supplies are available, as is often the case, we can use the somewhat simpler bias arrangement of Fig. 7.50(e). This circuit is an implementation of Eq. (7.137), with VG replaced by VSS. Resistor RG establishes a dc ground at the gate and presents a high input resistance to a signal source that may be connected to the gate through a coupling capacitor.

Expansion note: why the gate sits at 0 V dc

RG connects the gate to ground, and the gate draws no current. No current means no drop across RG, so the dc gate voltage equals ground. The source then sits one VGS below ground, and RS runs from there down to the negative supply.

Quoted · p. 449
VG=VGS+RSID
(7.137)
Quoted · choosing RD, p. 451

… resistor RD is selected to be as large as possible to obtain high gain but small enough to allow for the desired signal swing at the drain while keeping the MOSFET in saturation at all times.

How the book sizes swing room Example 7.11, p. 452

Quoted

Observe that the dc voltage at the drain (+10 V) allows for a positive signal swing of +5 V (i.e., up to VDD) and a negative signal swing of 4 V [i.e., down to (VG−Vt)].

The full Example 7.11 (single-supply design, Fig. 7.51) is quoted under Problem 7.92 above.

Headroom and legroom §7.1.7, p. 380; §7.2.1, p. 384

Summarized

The bias point needs room for the drain signal on both sides: too close to VDD and the positive peaks clip as the MOSFET cuts off (“headroom”); too close to the triode boundary and the negative peaks drive it into triode (“legroom”). For a given RD, the book recommends placing Q as close to the triode edge as the required negative swing allows (Fig. 7.9). In instantaneous terms (p. 384): vDS must not fall below vGS by more than Vt, and must stay below VDD (Fig. 7.12).

Expansion note: what a symmetric swing requires

A swing written as ± a peak value means the drain must move that far both up and down from its dc level. Going up, it must stay below the positive supply; going down, it must stay above the triode edge. Both limits have to hold at once.
